TREES AND SHRUBS.
The weather for some time back has been unusually severe—frost, snow, sleet, and rain having often been experienced within the compass of twenty four hours; consequently outdoor labour and the pursuits of all kinds have been considerably retarded in progress, but now that spring has set in we anticipate an improvement in the weather to enable cultivators to prepare the ground and insert their seeds and plants with some reasonable prospect of success. One great drawback to the development of trees and shrubs about large towns is the smoky atmosphere with which they are surrounded, and we have noticed this in particular in Glasgow and its immediate vicinity. This is to be regretted, as shrubs occupy a high place in the embellishment of towns and villa gardens where they thrive, and if any one could mature a plan for consuming the smoke, it would not only be beneficial for vegetation, but also promote the health of the inhabitants to a great degree. Most people like trees, as a proof of which we have only to point to the many dead trees standing in and around the city which the owners seem reluctant to cut down. This, however, we for several reasons consider a mistake, as, from their cold wintry-looking appearance, minus the bark and foliage, they give a place a decidedly neglected ruined appearance, and consequently lessen its value in the market; and in many cases where such trees are standing along the sides of streets, roads, and drives, they form a source of danger to the inhabitants, in proof of which we lately saw a rotten branch snap and fall to the ground during a gale of wind near the west end of Sauchiehall Street. This is a very proper time to renovate such places, by stubbing out dead trees and shrubs and in all cases where it is desirable to have the ground replanted with healthy stuff to give the place a furnished ornamental appearance. But the question naturally suggests itself, What shall we plant with any reasonable prospect of success? This at first sight, and in view of the many failures which we have seen in smoky districts, seems rather puzzling, yet there are some trees and shrubs better adapted than others for such situations, and in order to make a selection we shall briefly specify a few of them. For some time back the great rage has been for planting conifers of recent introduction into this country, and although most of them are highly ornamental, yet as a general rule they are unsuitable for town planting, one of the principal reasons being that the surfaces of the leaves, bark, and buds are slightly coated with resinous matter, and in consequence of which they get gradually coated with soot, which sticks and adheres to the plants, and, if I may be allowed to use the expression, actually chokes them. On the other hand, as a general rule, trees and shrubs that are furnished with hard, smooth, glossy leaves, whether evergreen or deciduous, are much better adapted for such situations, and although they cannot be said to be proof against the inimical effects of a smoky atmosphere, yet from the formation of their foliage they admit of being washed and cleansed by every shower of rain, which has a salutary effect in promoting their growth and healthy development. Although it would be superfluous to give a full list of names, yet we may notice a few of them, and in doing so we may mention the best, and its many varieties as being exceptionally well suited for town and villa planting. The holly has this advantage, that it is thoroughly hardy and capable of growing in a great variety of soils, and whether planted in masses, or single specimens, or below the drip of trees to give a furnished

It bears pruning with impunity, and when planted in grounds of limited extent it can be pruned or cut back to keep it within bounds and in harmony with the surroundings, which is no small recommendation. Rhododendrons are looked upon by many as being only fit for planting upon rich, peaty soils, but our experience of this plant does not warrant such an assumption as being correct. The only soils which we have found inimical to their growth are stiff, plastic clay, and calcareous soils that contain a mixture of lime. In laying out the grounds about new buildings and suburban villas, care should be taken to remove all lime from the surface left by masons, in order to prevent it from getting mixed with the soil where these shrubs are to be planted, otherwise failure will be the result. With these exceptions, and by a little care and painstaking in breaking up and preparing the soil, they may be planted with success in towns and villas, and as they afford great variety in flower and foliage, we can recommend them as one of the best evergreens for such situations.

ABERDEEN, LEITH, AND MORAY FIRTH STEAM SHIPPING COMPANY.—The directors of the Aberdeen, Leith, and Moray Firth Steam Shipping Company, Limited, in their annual report, state that, notwithstanding the violent weather experienced on the coast, and the withdrawal of "Earnholm" and the chartering of another steamer, the past year has yielded satisfactory results. The disposable balance, after deduction of all amounts carried to depreciation and reserve funds, is £1,127 15s. 10d., out of which the directors propose to pay a dividend of 10 per cent. on the paid-up capital of the company, carrying forward £327 15s. 10d. to credit of profit and loss account.

MARCH 30, 1895.
EDINBURGH ARCHITECTURAL ASSOCIATION.
The members of the Edinburgh Architectural Association have visited Liberton and Upper Liberton, and were shown over Liberton House, the former residence of the Littles, the owners of the barony, by Mr. Godfrey Cunninghame, the present tenant and occupant. The attention of the members was directed, in the first place, to the general plan of the house, consisting of a main block of buildings at right angles to the road, with a circular turret or stair at each end of these, together with another block of buildings enclosing on three sides a small square courtyard, the fourth side being originally shut in by a wall and gateway of a defensive character. The special interest of Liberton House lay in the fact that it belonged to a transition period of Scottish domestic architecture, even in its latest phases, when any claim to be considered a fortress had not yet been abandoned, and when the state of society rendered it necessary to retain safeguards against sudden attack. Though disfigured by a subsequent alteration in the height of the windows, which had been considered too low, and by the pitch of the roof, which had been depressed, the outlines of the original elevation were still clearly traceable, and the "Nelson room," a comparatively recent date, was explained as probably arising out of structural necessity, and to introduce the half-timbered construction at least in Scotland, more common in the exterior than with the interior of buildings in which it occurs. At the close of the visit the president, Mr. W. W. Robertson, F.S.A.Scot., proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Cunninghame, which was cordially and duly acknowledged.

BATHING AT ABERDEEN.—The Aberdeen Town Council purpose building a new bathing station at the beach, at a cost of £10,000, and the council leasing or purchasing ground for the supply of granite for causewaying and other public purposes was considered at the last meeting of the Council, when it was resolved to instruct a committee to report as to providing additional accommodation at the municipal buildings, and also to obtain professional advice.
